National aggregate prevalence can be estimated when a combination of randomly sampled clinics and conveniently sampled clinics report Early Warning Indicators (EWIs). Data abstraction from antiretroviral therapy (ART) clinics and data quality assessments are essential components of this process. This annex outlines a method for expanding the monitoring of EWIs of HIV drug resistance through random sampling of ART clinics. This approach provides representative data while progressively scaling up monitoring to all clinics in a country. Random sampling allows countries to calculate a national prevalence estimate for each EWI. Conveniently available data from clinics can also be incorporated without compromising representativeness. Primary sampling refers to the selection of clinics, while secondary sampling refers to the selection of patients within a clinic. Ideally, quality-of-care indicators, including EWIs of HIV drug resistance, should be reported from all ART clinics in a country. In cases where this is not feasible, it is recommended to progressively expand EWI reporting using a multi-year scale-up approach. For example, a country may start by sampling 20% of clinics in Year 1, then expand coverage by an additional 20% each year until 100% coverage is achieved in Year 5. Clinics may be selected using a combination of convenience sampling and random sampling, with results summarized in a nationally representative manner through weighting. Convenience sampling may be used for clinics already reporting EWI data or those with readily available data, such as clinics with electronic medical records (EMRs). However, random sampling is recommended as the primary mode of clinic selection to ensure national representativeness. Representative sampling can be achieved through simple random sampling or stratified random sampling, with no more than one stratum (e.g., district or province) recommended. For example, in Year 1, Country Z monitors EWIs at five clinics with readily available data and four randomly sampled clinics. In Year 2, the country continues monitoring at these clinics and randomly samples four additional clinics to expand EWI uptake by 20%. This process is repeated annually until all clinics report EWIs by Year 5. After Year 5, all clinics continue to report EWIs annually. Data collection should rely on patient-level data from clinics. Abstracting data from a census of all eligible patients is strongly preferred. If a census is not possible, sampling of patient records (e.g., systematic or simple random sampling) at individual clinics achieves results generalizable to the entire eligible population at the clinic. Sample size calculations depend on the size of the eligible patient populations, which vary by EWI. For example, the eligible population for ART adherence proxy (on-time ARV drug pick-up) includes all eligible pediatric patients in care or receiving ART at the clinic. For total attrition from ART (adult), the eligible population includes all adults receiving ART at the end of the last reporting period plus those newly initiating ART during the current reporting period, excluding those known to have transferred out to another facility. Sample size calculations are designed to achieve 95% confidence intervals of ±7% for clinic-specific results. Once the sample size is determined, patient records are randomly sampled until the required sample size is reached. Records with missing or incomplete data should not be excluded. Each clinic calculates the EWIs and assigns the appropriate classification (red, amber, green, or grey). A grey classification is used if 30% or more of the required data is missing. It is not necessary to calculate a 95% confidence interval for the EWI to make a classification. The classifications are presented in a scorecard format to help program managers identify areas of greatest need and monitor improvements or declines over time. The scorecard also reflects whether any indicators cannot be measured at a specific ART clinic. At the national level, countries are encouraged to report the fractions of clinics achieving green, amber, red, and grey classifications for each indicator and for both adult and pediatric populations. Nationally representative prevalence estimates for each EWI can be calculated by data aggregation and weighting. Clinics with greater patient burdens are weighted more heavily than smaller clinics. However, if less than 70% of data are available for the nationally eligible population monitored by a specific indicator, aggregation should not be performed. A flowchart is provided to assess the feasibility of aggregation at the national level. Aggregated values for all EWIs except ARV medicine stock-out represent the proportion of the patient population in the country with the relevant outcome. For ARV medicine stock-out, the aggregated value represents the average proportion of months with stock-outs of routinely dispensed ARV drugs among clinics in the country during the reporting period.
